title: Kabir at the Guru's Feet
hookLine: a weaver lies down in the dark where his teacher will step
carry: bow low; the ego is the wall
tomorrow: Can a man who never learned to read be the real scholar?

cards: Before dawn, on the stone steps that run down to the Ganges at Kashi, a young weaver lies stretched across a step in the dark. He knows a well-known teacher, Ramananda, comes down here to bathe at this hour.
The teacher's foot comes down on him. Startled, Ramananda cries out the name of God: Ram, Ram. And the young man goes home holding those words as if they'd been handed to him on purpose.
That, tradition says, is how Kabir got his teacher.

teach.b: Kabir is remembered as a weaver in Kashi, raised, tradition says, by a Muslim weaver couple, Niru and Nima. He wanted Ramananda as his guru, and how he got him is the lesson. He didn't argue his way in.
He lay down lower than the step, where the teacher's foot would land, and took the name that came with it, Ram, as his whole teaching. In Hindu life, the feet are where you meet a teacher.
Children touch their elders' feet; students bow at a guru's feet. Many explain it the same way: you lower your head, and the 'I' gets smaller.

Hindu teachers have a word for that 'I': ahamkara, the ego, literally the I-maker. Many bhakti teachers picture it as a wall between a person and God. Kabir put the turn in a doha, a two-line rhyming couplet.
This one begins, in Hindi, bura jo dekhan main chala. Roughly: I went out looking for the bad one, and couldn't find anyone.
Then I searched my own heart, and found no one worse than me. Notice the trap. The first line is the ego's favorite hunt: who's the problem here?
Found nobody. The second line turns the lamp around. It isn't saying you're terrible.
It's the same move as lying on the step: get lower than your own 'I'. The ego hunts outside; humility looks in. That's where Kabir says the work is, and where there's room for God.

how: Kabir's dohas are sung and quoted by followers of the Kabir Panth, in Hindu devotional singing, and in everyday talk; his verses are also kept in the Guru Granth Sahib. Touching an elder's or teacher's feet is a common Hindu sign of respect and humility.

o: a Sanskrit scholar who wrote long temple hymns
the teacher who cried Ram, Ram on the river steps
the weaver-poet of Kashi known for his two-line dohas

games.q: Kabir and his couplets — tap the pairs.
p: cried Ram, Ram on the steps
the weaver couple who raised him
I went out looking for the bad one

s: Hindu teachers call the ego ahamkara, the I-maker
true: aham means I, and Kabir got lower than his own.
in today's doha, the search finds someone worse than the speaker
he finds nobody outside, and no one worse than himself inside.
touching an elder's feet is a way of praising yourself
it lowers the head and the 'I': a bow to the teacher, as Kabir lay under Ramananda's foot.

games.q: you're Kabir, a young weaver who wants a teacher. the teacher you want comes down the steps to the river before dawn. what do you do?
o: wait at his door and ask politely.
lie down on the steps in the dark.
games.why: tradition says he lay on the steps, lower than the teacher's foot; Ramananda stepped on him and cried Ram, Ram, and Kabir took those words as his teaching.

practice: The next time you greet an elder, a grandparent or a teacher, try the old gesture of pranam: a bow, folded hands, or touching their feet if your family does. If not, simply bow your head inwardly.

Then bring to mind one person you've been quietly blaming, and turn Kabir's lamp around: what did I bring to this? If you pray, offer what you found to God; if you don't, let your 'I' be a little smaller for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi who got his guru by lying under his feet, and whose doha turns the hunt for the bad one back on the hunter.

carryVoice: Your line: bow low; the ego is the wall. Kabir lay down under his teacher's foot, and found the bad one in his own heart. See you tomorrow.
